outcomes.text: Use omission, replacement or a question to test a group in context.
Use brackets and branches to identify exactly which words belong together.
Explain how two groupings of the same words can lead to two readings.

opening.prompt: In “Jo checked the old clock”, which words can “it” replace to make “Jo checked it”?

options.feedback: Those words identify the person and action. Both stay in the new sentence.
“It” takes the place of all three words after “checked”.
That replacement would leave “the” before “it”.

opening.prompt: In “Luz waited by the lake”, which words answer “Where did Luz wait?”

options.feedback: That names the landmark. The question asks for the location relative to it.
This includes the action and leaves out the landmark.
The complete answer includes the relation “by” and the landmark “the lake”.

opening.prompt: In [behind [the green door]], which words are inside the inner brackets?

options.feedback: The inner opening bracket comes before “the” and its closing bracket follows “door”.
The outer brackets enclose the whole location.
Those words cross the inner boundary.

opening.prompt: In “Rae saw the cyclist with binoculars”, could the last words describe Rae’s equipment or the cyclist’s equipment?

options.feedback: That is the likely everyday reading. The words can also describe a cyclist who has binoculars.
The last words can also describe how Rae saw the cyclist.
The last words can describe the seeing or join the words that identify the cyclist.

opening.prompt: In “Kai rested under the bench”, which words can be omitted to leave “Kai rested”?

options.feedback: That leaves “under” without its landmark.
The whole location can be left out.
That would leave “Kai the bench”.

closing.prompt: “Emil left before the concert” can become “Emil left”. What does that support?

options.text: The whole time phrase is an optional group here
options.feedback: Leaving out the whole time phrase still gives a complete sentence.
The example removes “before the concert” together.

options.text: “The concert” is the whole time phrase
options.feedback: The time phrase also includes “before”.

closing.prompt: In [beside [the paper lantern]], which words must one node reach to represent just the landmark?

options.feedback: That is the larger location.
The node reaches all and only the inner group.
This leaves out “the”, which is inside the inner group.

closing.prompt: PHRASE-a branches to “under” and PHRASE-b. PHRASE-b branches to “the”, “wooden” and “bridge”. What does PHRASE-a immediately dominate?

options.feedback: PHRASE-a reaches the bridge words through another node.
Those three branches come from PHRASE-b.
Those are the two elements one branch below PHRASE-a.

closing.prompt: In “Ari waited beside the bus that goes downtown”, the last words identify which bus. Why does “beside the bus” end too early for the location group?

options.text: The full landmark includes “that goes downtown”
options.feedback: On this reading the descriptive words are part of the landmark and therefore part of the whole location.

options.text: A location group must contain the verb “waited”
options.feedback: “Waited” describes the action. The location begins at “beside”.

options.text: The words “the bus” cannot form a phrase anywhere
options.feedback: They can form a phrase in other contexts. Here the specified reading requires the longer landmark.

closing.prompt: In “Eva interviewed the reporter with a recorder”, which group does “with a recorder” join if it identifies the person Eva interviewed?

options.feedback: That attachment would make the recorder part of how Eva conducted the interview.
The phrase helps identify the reporter by saying who had the recorder.
The reading describes the reporter, the person being interviewed.
